bib.title: AI co-mathematician: Accelerating mathematicians with agentic AI

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AI co-mathematician: Accelerating mathematicians with agentic AI", Daniel Zheng, Ingrid von Glehn, Yori Zwols et al. (Google DeepMind; corresponding authors Zheng and Pushmeet Kohli). arXiv:2605.06651v2 [cs.AI], 13 May 2026 (header date 2026-05-07). Preprint, not peer reviewed. Limited initial release only.

COVERAGE: All 23 pages, 74,847 chars. Pages 1-17 are body, 17-18 are acknowledgments and contributions, 18-23 are references (skimmed). There are NO appendices. I also viewed the page 14 image to read the Figure 5 bar values, which are not in the extracted text. Figures 1-4 are architecture diagrams; I read only their captions.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: The system scored 48% on FrontierMath Tier 4, which the authors call a new high score among AI systems. It solved 23 of 48 problems (the 2 public samples are excluded). The 48 are Epoch AI's problems, and the full Tier 4 has 50.
  number: 23/48 = 48%
  setup: Epoch AI ran it blind. They entered the problems and retrieved answers through the UI, and the developers saw neither the problems nor the workspaces. It ran in final-answer mode with a 48-hour limit. It uses its own tools and has no cap on model calls or tokens. Epoch's standard harness has a Python tool and a hard token limit.
  quote: "correctly solving 23 problems out of 48, once the two public sample problems are excluded, an accuracy of 48%."
  where: p.14
- claim: The base model, Gemini 3.1 Pro, scored 19% on the same benchmark. The paper credits the gain to parallel branches, enforced review cycles and tools.
  number: 19%
  setup: Same Tier 4 evaluation. The paper does not say whether Gemini 3.1 Pro ran in Epoch's standard harness.
  quote: "this is a significant increase over the Gemini 3.1 Pro base model which achieved 19% accuracy and which the AI co-mathematician is based on"
  where: p.14
- claim: Three solved problems had not been solved by any earlier evaluated system, and two problems that some earlier system had solved were missed.
  number: 3 new, 2 missed
  setup: Compared with the Epoch leaderboard at the time. Counts only.
  quote: "The problems solved correctly included three problems which had not been solved by any previously evaluated system, though the AI co-mathematician also failed to solve two problems which had been previously solved by at least one system."
  where: p.14
- claim: On an internal benchmark, the system beat a single call to Gemini 3.1 Pro and a single call to Gemini Deep Think. The text gives no numbers; the Figure 5 bars read 57% (3.1 Pro), 70% (3.1 Deep Think) and 87% (co-mathematician).
  number: 87% vs 70% vs 57% (from the figure image only, not the text)
  setup: 100 unleaked research-level problems with code-checkable answers, supplied by professional mathematicians. Run with a 24-hour limit. It uses much more compute than a single call. Internal agents are Gemini 3.1 Pro, and the prover agent can use Deep Think.
  quote: "an internal benchmark consisting of 100 unleaked, research-level mathematics problems with code-checkable answers, sourced from professional mathematicians." Fig 5 caption: "Accuracy scores for Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Deep Think, and the AI co-mathematician (also based on Gemini 3.1), on an internal research mathematics benchmark."
  where: p.13-14
- claim: Early users resolved or advanced real problems, including Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.10 (M. Lackenby), which asked whether every finite group admits a "just finite presentation". The answer was yes, and Lackenby completed the proof. Two Stirling-coefficient conjectures (Bérczi) got proofs that are still under human review. A Hamiltonian-systems lemma (Rezchikov) was essentially resolved. The paper has no count of open problems solved.
  number: none (3 case studies)
  setup: Small limited release. The paper says results were produced independently by the mathematicians without GDM supervision. Users reported mixed satisfaction, and Rezchikov's comparisons with other AI systems were uncontrolled.
  quote: "His work led to a resolution of an open question (Problem 21.10 from the Kourovka Notebook)." Also: "other users have found it less effective for their work."
  where: p.10-12
- claim: Compute cost per attempt is described only qualitatively, as comparable to a long AI-assisted software-engineering session.
  number: none
  setup: No explicit inference limits in benchmark mode.
  quote: "each attempt uses a broadly comparable number of model and tool calls to a long AI-assisted software engineering session"
  where: p.13

ARCHITECTURE
- It is a harness over standard commercial Gemini models, with no custom training: "does not rely on any custom model behavior or training."
- A hierarchy of agents writes to a shared file system and talks over an internal messaging system. The user talks mainly to a top-level project coordinator agent.
- Onboarding is a dialogue. The coordinator clarifies intent, writes the central research question and goals, and the user approves them. Work only then starts.
- Each approved goal gets one or more parallel workstreams. Each has its own workstream coordinator agent that runs a linear sequence of actions and delegates to specialised sub-agents: literature review, coding agent, Gemini Deep Think prover, and a parallel code-execution tool on cloud machines. Workstreams can be added at any time and can fail with a visible warning.
- Each workstream outputs a compiled LaTeX "working paper" with exposition, margin annotations linking claims to the workspace, and internal links. Incremental reports are visible while work runs.
- Hard programmatic constraints: the coding agent cannot mark code finished until tests pass and a reviewer agent accepts the code and the golden values. Several AI reviewer agents can check references, code and logic. They persist across rounds, and all must approve before a workstream is complete. If review stalls, the workstream escalates to the project coordinator, is marked unfinished and flags the user.
- Failed workstreams and dead ends are kept as permanent records ("negative space").
- Progressive disclosure: the user sees the coordinator and can drill into any sub-agent.
- Human steering: the user can message the coordinator at any time. The coordinator asks the user for help when stuck, for example for a pruning heuristic in the sofa-problem walkthrough.
- Benchmark mode: no onboarding dialogue, a single hard-coded goal of "solve the problem", and a fixed time limit (24 h internal, 48 h FrontierMath). The system "occasionally continues beyond this."
- Current sub-agents are plain LLM calls (including Deep Think). AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof and Aletheia are NOT used. All proofs are informal.
- The seven design principles: maths beyond proofs; iterative refinement of intent; native artifacts; asynchronous steering; progressive disclosure; tracking uncertainty; preserving failed explorations.

LIMITS
- Reviewer-pleasing false consensus: the system can converge on a flawed argument whose errors the reviewers can no longer detect ("relatively rare").
- Non-termination: review can loop forever and degrade into a "death spiral" of hallucinated reasoning. Users learned to spot it and trust that output less.
- Autonomy versus control: model judgment on unplanned difficulties is "far behind human capabilities."
- Well-typeset LaTeX suggests rigor that is not there.
- Risks to the literature and to peer review: a flood of plausible but shallow papers, and a verification burden on human referees.
- Lackenby: "the system works best when the user is familiar with the area." Bérczi: "It's not trivial how to use this now."
- Cost: the system "likely has a higher inference cost than previously evaluated systems", so the 48% is not a compute-matched comparison with token-capped harnesses. The ablation shows only the Gemini 3.1 Pro baseline, with no component ablations, no variance or seeds, and no cost figures.
- The internal benchmark is private and not reproducible. The paper gives no counts for open problems solved. There is no human-interaction benchmark, and the authors say none exists for research mathematics.
- Access is limited, and the code is not released.
- Dating: leaderboard claims are as of May 2026 and have probably been overtaken by November 2026.

BUILDS ON: Aletheia [17], AlphaEvolve [18,19], AlphaProof [23], Gemini Deep Think, Epoch AI's FrontierMath (Glazer et al. 2024). The interaction model draws on coding agents (Antigravity, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex). The design philosophy credits Pólya 1954, Lakatos 1976, Thurston, and Putnam on quasi-empirical mathematics. The failure modes cite prover-verifier dynamics (Dang et al. 2026) and Kontorovich 2025.

CODE: none.

FIGURES (from the PDF; the figures.py captions script returned nothing)
- Fig 1, p.5: agent organisation in a workspace (user, project coordinator, workstream coordinators, sub-agents). Useful for the comparison with a research-agent architecture.
- Fig 3, p.7: the project coordinator schedules workstreams per goal, with incremental reports and failure warnings.
- Fig 4, p.8: the trajectory of one workstream, from literature search to review to "complete".
- Fig 5, p.14: bar chart, internal evaluation (100 questions). Bars 57%, 70%, 87%.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction was clean. The 87/70/57 values come from viewing the figure image, not from extracted text, so they have no verbatim text quote. Page-number citations are from the PDF page footers.
